name: Kibala
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Kibala/Ngoya: Glottolog refs are Koelle 1854 wordlist and Jordan & Manuel 2016 sociolinguistic survey; no phonology found

new_statements.quote: um eventual índice de caso tonal, que indica uma determinada função sintática do nome (predicado, sujeito, objeto, etc.) e que é apenas constituído por um tom flutuante alto ou baixo, i.e, um auto-segmento subespecificado composto pelo único traço tonal [...] || Nas três línguas, observa-se mudanças tonais vinculadas a diferentes funções do substantivo que são chamadas “casos tonais” (Daeleman, 1983). As principais funções sintáticas que determinam casos tonais são as posições predicado, sujeito e objeto.
new_statements.translation: a possible tonal-case index, which indicates a given syntactic function of the noun (predicate, subject, object, etc.) and which consists solely of a floating high or low tone, i.e. an underspecified autosegment made up of the single tonal feature [...] || In the three languages one observes tonal changes tied to the different functions of the noun, which are called 'tonal cases' (Daeleman 1983). The main syntactic functions that determine tonal cases are the predicate, subject and object positions.

As principais funções sintáticas que determinam casos tonais são as posições pr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kibala (Ebo dialect; Ipala-Hepo in the 2013 paper) is described as a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language with floating-tone 'tonal cases', progressive H spreading, final lowering and downstep, plus lexical and derived vowel length (long noun-initial vowels from mora re-association). Neither first-hand description mentions word stress or accent at all, so no stress position can be stated; the language should be filed as tonal with no stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal exceptions: augment /o-/ dropped in predicative case except before monosyllabic class 9/10 stems (p. 257); Kibala vs Umbundu differ in presence of compensatory lengthening (2013, §14).
new_statements.domain_note: Both papers analyse the noun in three syntactic positions (predicate, subject, object); tone rules are stated at word level with one post-lexical sandhi rule (2013, ANG 7). Data: 2010 fieldwork, Ebo/Hepo variety; 2013 tonal annotations perceptually checked by Huta-Mukana and vowel durations instrumentally checked (SIL Speech Analyzer).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Kibala' (bolo1261, ISO blv, formerly reference name 'Bolo'; ISO CR 2016-035) = Ngoya = Ipala; 'Bolo/Libolo' proper is a peripheral dialect. The 2011 paper describes the Ebo (Kibala-Ebo) dialect and the 2013 paper the Ipala-Hepo (Hebó) dialect, both central varieties of the same language; Glottolog lists no dialect-level glottocodes. Do not confuse with Kimbundu (kimb1241/kmb) or with Songo/Sama.

sources.note: Nothing about stress/acento. Kibala-Ebo is described as a two-tone (H/L) language: floating H/L 'tonal case' indices marking predicate/subject/object (pp. 255, 259-262), three extrinsically ordered tone rules for Kibala-Ebo (initial raising, final lowering, downstep; p. 261), and lexical/derived vowel length before prenasalised consonants, after palatalised/labialised consonants and before monosyllabic stems (p. 259).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority (submitter Linda Jordan). 2016. Change Request 2016-035: Bolo [blv] -> Kibala (adopted 2017-01-31). 6 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Gives dialects (Kibala/Ipala central; Hebó, Ucela, Mbwĩ, Bolo, Sende peripheral) and the full bibliography: Angenot et al. 2011, Angenot/Angenot/Huta-Mukana 2013, Jordan & Manuel 2016, Menezes 2011, Vinte e Cinco 1992.

sources.citation: Angenot, Jean-Pierre, Geralda de Lima Vitor Angenot & Daniel Mutombo Huta-Mukana. 2013. Comparison between the Ipala-Ngoya, Kimbundu and Umbundu tone-cases systems. Revista Eletrônica Língua Viva (UNIR, Guajará-Mirim) 3(1), 28 pp. (footer prints 'p. 15-17'; Glottolog lists pp. 1-28).
sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent (the words do not occur). Ipala-Hepo dialect, 2010 fieldwork with instrumental vowel-duration check: seven ordered tone rules (progressive H spreading, lowering, vowel coalescence, floating-tone association with compensatory lengthening, falling, downstepping, sandhi raising; PDF p. 6), tone-case derivations (pp. 7-8), and 'In Ipala the surface initial vowel of a noun which is always long is originated from a compensatory lengthening caused by the re-association of the mora of a preceding case index floating tone or augment' (§14, PDF p. 24).
